Drugs in the City

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Do you know where your kids are on a Friday night...

Summary:
An investigative expose of the free availability of hard drugs in upmarket clubs, as well as the amount of underage (minors) children who get access to the clubs, and to the liquor and drugs being sold there.

Further information:
We all know that drugs are a problem in South Africa. But how serious is this problem in upmarket areas, and what effect does it have on school children? We will spend one weekend visiting these clubs with a hidden cam.
We start off the story with a boy who was expelled from a fourways highschool for using drugs. He now makes a living selling drugs (mostly to school children) – he advertises on instagram and facebook and the children can order via cellphone. We plan to use a 21 year old (who looks young) dressed up as a school girl. She'll sms and ask him to deliver the drugs to her at the garage next to the school during break. We will then film this transaction and confront him later in the story.
Then we follow a typical school kids night out on the town. Early in the evening they all congregate at a O'Hagans where no id is required and they can sit and drink on the veranda. Nigerians selling drugs do their rounds every now and then going from table to table to greet their regular customers and fish for new ones. If anybody needs drugs they pay him and he goes back into the bar. He will phone a second person who will then deliver the drugs to the correct table. The owners are not part of the drug dealing, but know all about it as they are being threatened with closure if they don't allow the pushers to deal there. They even have to supply the pushers with free drinks and food while they are on the premises.
The kids will hang out here until closing time when they will move on to one of the venues who are still open after midnight – mostly ESP, Billy's and Sunrise. Here the drugs are more readily available and they get access to the clubs by paying bribes. When these clubs close, between 2 and 4 am they start coming to Aruba or stay at Sunrise. At both these clubs the drugs are sold in the parking lots with big numbers of drug pushers approaching any vehicles arriving. If caught these pushers all claim to be independent, but in fact they work for the club owners. The club orders the drugs in bulk, they then cut it into smaller bags which they give to the pushers outside to sell on a commission basis. Inside the club you can also drugs from the bouncers or waiters and even pay with your credit card – it will be billed as drinks or food from the restaurant. The kids will do the drugs in the toilets, but at Aruba and Sunrise it is not uncommon to see users snort Cat or Coke on the tables where they are sitting. It is also not uncommon to see someone (minor or otherwise) double clutching – this is a form of over dosage on the current fashionable drug called Disco biscuits (a mixture of weed and Cat). The person looks passed out but is in fact tripping. An ambulance from Honeydew does the rounds twice a night to pick up over dose emergencies . We are trying to get permission to send the presenter with the ambulance one night to see how many of these case there are.
These clubs close at 8 in the morning and you often seen kids sitting lost and stoned on the sidewalks with nowhere to go – apparently they all told their parents that they were sleeping over at each others houses.
People who will be interviewed on camera:
1. Parents of a child hooked on heroine and who has destroyed them financially.
2. Nigerian who sells drugs at one of these clubs. He will explain that they work for the club and how the system works.
3. Bouncer at one club who will explain why drugs can be sold so freely (police involvement)
4. Ambulance driver explaining how common it is to pick up underage children who took too many drugs.
5. Confrontational interview with boy who sells drugs to school children
6. Confrontational with restaurant manager on why they serve alcohol without asking for id's

Extra Budget Items:
Buying of 4 bags of CAT, 1x Crack pipe plus rock and two Strawberry Quik Straws

Expert:
Mr. Quintin van Kerken CEO Anti Drug Alliance
Mr. Hein Pienaar Former Club DJ

Locations:
Gauteng, mostly West Rand, Fourways

Hidden Camera: Yes
Reason for hidden camera: To film drugs being sold and used in clubs.
To trap drug pusher selling to school kids

Legal: Yes
Reason for legal: Possible Right of Reply issues. Purchasing of drugs issues.

Press Release:


Drugs in the city
Just how easy is it to buy hard drugs in Johannesburg’s northern suburbs? No more dimly lit alleys, shady dealers or gang-controlled neighbourhoods. It’s as simple as swiping your credit card at some of Johannesburg’s foremost night spots. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Drugs in the City

Visual
Audio
Devi at computer
It all started last year after we received information about a school boy who seemed to be openly advertising drugs on his instagram page.

V/o
The whole idea of social media helping children to get access to dangerous drugs without their parents knowing is quite disturbing, but as the chances of cannabis being legalised seems to be growing, it also seems that it is losing its popularity with the party crowd. We spoke to a regular drug user who's been part of the scene for a number of years.
Little miss X
They don't even know anything about dagga or where to get it, and they don't particularly care. But crystal meth is seen as quite swanky these days and quite trendy and very popular. Chrystal Meths is now – I would say – South Africa's most lucrative drug, most popular drug, most addictive drug...
Devi at computer
But even worse than that is this email that's been doing the rounds for a few years now about a flavoured form of crystal meth known as strawberry quik.
V/o
It looks just like a well-known candy straw and the warnings claim that it is a way to specifically target very young children with this brain damaging drug.

But Wikipedia and anti-drug sources on the web have all slated these warnings as nonsense. In the 8 years since the rumours started, no hard proof has ever been found anywhere in the world that it actually exists.
Quintin van Kerken runs a local NGO and has, among other things, been working with young addicts for years.


Quintin van Kerken
It's an urban legend. It crops up... every couple of months I get a journalist or a parent phoning me going “oh God, have you heard about this?”. Really, it's nothing to be concerned about. I think it's more of an urban legend than anything else.


School coming out
But, even if Strawbery Quik is a myth, the tragic fact is that hard drugs are already a reality in our high-schools. Randpark High in Joburg's Northern suburbs is no exception. Here, it all seems to start at the petrol station across the road from the school.
V/o
We went there on a Friday afternoon, filming with our cell phones. We couldn't get close enough to film the detail but we certainly saw teens interacting with various men hanging around the petrol station. The fore-court workers told us that the men are Nigerian drug dealers and that some children come here every afternoon to buy drugs.

This boy, who changed into private clothes as soon as he arrived, was pointed out by some workers as being a king-pin in the dealings, assisted by this girl.
V/o
The owner of the petrol station declined to speak on camera fearing for his safety, but Shell SA did give us permission to set up hidden cameras on the Monday. But on Monday it was clear that someone had warned the dealers. The same teens arrived, but the Nigerians were absent.
Devi @ Petrol Station
On the face of it, it looks perfectly innocent, except we know what happens behind those post boxes. And what boggles my mind is that 2 months ago the police were here and the drug dealers were back in action the same day.
V/o
But, 50m from the pumps, we saw the dealers hiding their stuff in the bushes in case anyone searched them.
Soundup
There they are hiding their stuff...
V/o
Driving around the neighbourhood we were offered crystal meth in no less than 6 places. We also got phone numbers from 4 dealers who said they would deliver...
UPSOUND
Have you got crystal?
Yes...
Where is the money?
I've got it here...
Yes I do crystal
V/o
All the experts tell us that the clubs are the real evil when it comes to drugs and underage children.
V/o
Hein Pienaar is a former DJ who still frequents the different clubs.
Hein Pienaar – Former DJ
I find underage and very young, all the time. Maybe I've just grown older, but they are very young. You can see it.
V/o
And it seems some clubs are specifically targeting underage children.
Little miss X
It's very common to see underage kids in nightclubs. I'd say there are a few in Johannesburg, especially at the moment, that are in excess 70% minor.
Hein Pienaar – Former DJ
Once I was invited to a CD launch and before the guy who actually launched the CD even did his presentation and his launch, I actually left. It was so disturbing to see how cooked these kids were.
V/o
Crystal meth is a party drug – It lessens the effect of alcohol, increases your libido and keeps you awake for days.
Quintin
With a drug like CAT you can go 6, 7, 8 days without sleeping. No problem. It just depends how much you use.
Little Miss X
I've heard of people staying awake for 8 days which I didn't even think was a physical possibility.
V/o
But to stay awake you need money, and if you're underage, the addiction could be difficult to sustain.
Quintin
It's very easy for a girl to get a drink. She bats her eyelids a bit, and suddenly someone is going to buy her a drink. So, she wants drugs... it's a sexual favour.
Little Miss X
I've seen young girls, between the ages of... all of them underage, 13, 14, 15 year olds, visibly, some of these clubs have unisex bathrooms, the cubicle door will be left open and they're on their knees giving a blow-job. That's the going rate. A BJ for a pill, so a disco biscuit, or maybe an MDMA capsule...which is something that can be purchased for a conservative R50.
V/o
Not something a teenager would want their parents to know. And so they simply don’t go home for the entire weekend.
Devi Link
This is Aruba Lounge, a nightclub just behind the Dome in Johannesburg. They open from Thursday night to Sunday night. Because they only close at 8am customers from other nightclubs usually end up here.
V/o
Here, you don't have to look for the drug dealers after dark. They will find you.
UPSOUND
Have you got Cat?
Yes. How much?
R200
V/o
The increase in drug dealers got so bad that the centre hired a security team to specifically get rid of the dealers. The head of the company met up with us in a quiet park one morning.
Viktor
The problems start on Thursday because the club is open on Thursday. Thursday, Friday, Saturday... I call them Hell Nights... for me.
V/o
Victor realised that a number of these dealers actually work for Aruba, posing as car guards.
Viktor
I spoke to the owner. He said “Vic, listen here, these people are working for me. I don't see anything wrong because they are car guards.”
V/o
Victor is not the only person who believes that Aruba is connected to the drug dealing.
Quintin
The drugs around there, it's just crazy. You're getting drugs inside, outside, all over. Aruba is very much a hotspot, a centre point of where a lot of stuff is happening.
V/o
The Owner declined to speak on camera, but sent us a long email saying that they are opposed to any form of substance abuse. And that they find any allegations of people being able to buy drugs inside, and paying with a credit card inconceivable. So, our investigators went in to see for themselves.
Investigator
In you went...??

We asked the waiter if we can buy drugs and pay with our card, and he said yes, except, outside you would pay for CAT... for one bag you would pay R200. But if you want to pay by credit card you have got to take a minimum of two. You've got to buy for R400, for the luxury of paying by card inside. Which we said is fine. And then, maybe an hour later the waiter came and said the good stuff is there and he can bring it. He brought the card machine. I swiped my card, and when he gave me my slip it was billed as Aruba lounge drinks and then, wrapped inside that, was the 2 bags that we bought.

V/o
A week later, the two investigators went back, repeated the experiment, and got the same result.
Quintin
Some of the parents think that as long as my child doesn't have cash, it's okay. Because you need cash to buy drugs. Don't be fooled, you go into the club, you swipe your card, you get your drugs.
V/o

Important to not say we here. Changed to “they”. Wynand.
We asked Quintin to use one of his field testing kits to tell us whether the powder in the bags THEY bought was in fact Cat.
UPSOUND
Test
Definitely CAT
V/o
During our investigation we also kept asking people about the Strawberry Quik rumours. After a lot of secrecy, our agents finally sourced two straws of what was claimed to be the real thing. A bit sceptical, Quintin agreed to test it
UPSOUND
Probably just bought sherbet...
Quintin



??

Fuck me... Can we reshoot that Strawberry Quick? I'm going to have to do a retraction right there.

You're looking a bit visibly shaken here.

To be very honest with you, I am very shaken. We do have a positive for it. This tells me there definitely is crystal meth in there that has been cut down, possibly with a little bit of coke as well.

This makes me very, very, very scared.

What I am seeing here is this is a way to get children to use drugs very quickly. It's sugar, it's food colouring, and it's crystal meth.

It's available in different flavours, so if strawberry doesn't do it for you...

… well, then another flavour would.

But if this has to get onto the market, we are going to get a very, very serious problem with the children in our country.

This is possibly the scariest thing that I've seen in my life because it tells you how low a drug dealer is willing to stoop.
They're now in primary schools. Let's get them hooked at 8, 9 and 10 and you have a client for life... well, depending how long their life lasts.

After a lot of secrecy, our agents finally sourced two straws of what was claimed to be the real thing. A bit sceptical, Quintin agreed to test it UPSOUND Probably just bought sherbet... Quintin ?? Fuck me... Can we reshoot that Strawberry Quick? I'm going to have to do a retraction right there. You're looking a bit visibly shaken here. To be very honest with you, I am very shaken. We do have a positive for it. This tells me there definitely is crystal meth in there that has been cut down, possibly with a little bit of coke as well. This makes me very, very, very scared. What I am seeing here is this is a way to get children to use drugs very quickly. It's sugar, it's food colouring, and it's crystal meth. It's available in different flavours, so if strawberry doesn't do it for you... … well, then another flavour would. But if this has to get onto the market, we are going to get a very, very serious problem with the children in our country. This is possibly the scariest thing that I've seen in my life because it tells you how low a drug dealer is willing to stoop. They're now in primary schools. Let's get them hooked at 8, 9 and 10 and you have a client for life... well, depending how long their life lasts. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Do you know where your kids are on a Friday night...
metadata.Summary: An investigative expose of the free availability of hard drugs in upmarket clubs, as well as the amount of underage (minors) children who get access to the clubs, and to the liquor and drugs being sold there.
metadata.Further information: We all know that drugs are a problem in South Africa. But how serious is this problem in upmarket areas, and what effect does it have on school children? We will spend one weekend visiting these clubs with a hidden cam. We start off the story with a boy who was expelled from a fourways highschool for using drugs. He now makes a living selling drugs (mostly to school children) – he advertises on instagram and facebook and the children can order via cellphone. We plan to use a 21 year old (who looks young) dressed up as a school girl. She'll sms and ask him to deliver the drugs to her at the garage next to the school during break. We will then film this transaction and confront him later in the story. Then we follow a typical school kids night out on the town. Early in the evening they all congregate at a O'Hagans where no id is required and they can sit and drink on the veranda. Nigerians selling drugs do their rounds every now and then going from table to table to greet their regular customers and fish for new ones. If anybody needs drugs they pay him and he goes back into the bar. He will phone a second person who will then deliver the drugs to the correct table. The owners are not part of the drug dealing, but know all about it as they are being threatened with closure if they don't allow the pushers to deal there. They even have to supply the pushers with free drinks and food while they are on the premises. The kids will hang out here until closing time when they will move on to one of the venues who are still open after midnight – mostly ESP, Billy's and Sunrise. Here the drugs are more readily available and they get access to the clubs by paying bribes. When these clubs close, between 2 and 4 am they start coming to Aruba or stay at Sunrise. At both these clubs the drugs are sold in the parking lots with big numbers of drug pushers approaching any vehicles arriving. If caught these pushers all claim to be independent, but in fact they work for the club owners. The club orders the drugs in bulk, they then cut it into smaller bags which they give to the pushers outside to sell on a commission basis. Inside the club you can also drugs from the bouncers or waiters and even pay with your credit card – it will be billed as drinks or food from the restaurant. The kids will do the drugs in the toilets, but at Aruba and Sunrise it is not uncommon to see users snort Cat or Coke on the tables where they are sitting. It is also not uncommon to see someone (minor or otherwise) double clutching – this is a form of over dosage on the current fashionable drug called Disco biscuits (a mixture of weed and Cat). The person looks passed out but is in fact tripping. An ambulance from Honeydew does the rounds twice a night to pick up over dose emergencies . We are trying to get permission to send the presenter with the ambulance one night to see how many of these case there are. These clubs close at 8 in the morning and you often seen kids sitting lost and stoned on the sidewalks with nowhere to go – apparently they all told their parents that they were sleeping over at each others houses. People who will be interviewed on camera: 1. Parents of a child hooked on heroine and who has destroyed them financially. 2. Nigerian who sells drugs at one of these clubs. He will explain that they work for the club and how the system works. 3. Bouncer at one club who will explain why drugs can be sold so freely (police involvement) 4. Ambulance driver explaining how common it is to pick up underage children who took too many drugs. 5. Confrontational interview with boy who sells drugs to school children 6. Confrontational with restaurant manager on why they serve alcohol without asking for id's
